doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Best shooting moments: the Joe Williams film and Fathead Newman
summary: Rowe and Crohn recall the Basie band concert filming with Joe Williams, and Crohn recalls moments when everything came together.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: So what’s the best circumstances you’ve ever been shooting at — the most — like everything came together. I mean I know what I thought.

Well the Joe Williams film was — I’ll never forget that moment when, for those people who are watching, we filmed the Basie band with Joe Williams at the college. And that night, when everything finally came together and the band started and I was standing there with nothing to do.
Because you had done everything else up to then.

I had no idea what to do but I was like so overwhelmed at that time with all these booms going all over the place and the place was overflowing. I remember we had to find another room and we fed a thing to the camera so these people could watch it. Like wow, this was fantastic.

Yeah, I love the Joe Williams film, and I love showing it. And to me, see you stopped working then but I didn’t. I was nervous, I was in the control room. And then we still had to edit and everything. But I’m very happy with what came out, though I look at it and I wish I had Joe for a longer period of time. We only had him for two days and there was a lot more things I would have liked to have gotten. But I think it works. But you know I look at the film I did on Fathead [Newman] which is just a very short thing. I think that’s beautiful because it captured Fathead. So I don’t know, and there are things that will never see the light of day but something just came together. It’s the same thing I talk about making — people talk about making music. Sometimes I’m shooting, just shooting, and something takes over and it’s not me that’s doing the shooting, I’m just getting what I’m meant to be getting. That sometimes happens in editing too. So I’m not sure that it’s any one thing, but there are moments that just come together. When I was shooting the shamans in Ecuador and there’s a scene where they’re hunting with blowguns, and there’s just some footage in there that’s beautiful. And somehow it’s beautiful because everything came together just right. Or they’re fishing with their hands and the rushing water is going by and I’m holding the camera an inch from the water while they’re fishing with their hands. So I think you just get into the moment sometimes and whether it all makes it into a finished film or not, I don’t know.
